catalog_quote: Unfortunately, stress in Biloxi largely remains a mystery. The accent marks written by both Gatschet and Dorsey often vary even for the same word, making stress placement uncertain. However, both Gatschet and Dorsey often agree on stress placement in their transcriptions, both often showing a written stress mark over the final syllable of a word. Word-final stress, however, is unusual for Siouan languages, in which first- or second-syllable stress is the norm. There is the possibility that Biloxi stress placement had been affected by long-term contact with the western Muskogean languages, Choctaw and Chickasaw, both of which have predominantly syllable-final pitch accent.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No stress rule can be established for Biloxi (extinct since the 1930s, known almost entirely from Gatschet 1886 and Dorsey 1892-93 transcriptions whose accent marks are inconsistent); where the two transcribers agree, the mark is most often on the word-final syllable, which Kaufman flags as atypical for Siouan and possibly contact-induced. The same source records at least one pair distinguished only by Gatschet's stress mark (ksíhi 'crazy' vs ksihí 'evening', p. 89), and Dorsey & Swanton 1912 note clitic-conditioned accent shifts (xe 'affects the accent of the preceding word'; na 'attracts the accent'). Einaudi 1976: 21 (sec. 160) independently and explicitly declines to treat suprasegmentals for the same reason: 'In view of the erratic transcriptions of length and stress, no attempt will be made to deal with suprasegmental features.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Kaufman: final-syllable marking is a tendency, not a rule; transcriptions vary for the same word. Dorsey & Swanton 1912: sentence-final particles xe and na shift/attract the accent of the preceding word; grave accent on oral particles marks falling tone. Kaufman p.89: ksíhi 'crazy' vs ksihí 'evening' distinguished by stress mark in Gatschet.
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern written accent marks on words as transcribed in elicitation and texts (Gatschet 1886, Dorsey 1892-93; Haas & Swadesh 1934 for a few dozen words); no phonetic or phrase-level analysis is possible for this extinct language. Kaufman's 'stress' is the transcribers' acute accent; whether it was stress or pitch accent is itself left open (he compares Muskogean final pitch accent).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Biloxi proper (bilo1248, ISO bll), extinct; the corpus is Dorsey's 1892-93 Lecompte (Rapides Parish, Louisiana) material from Betsey Joe, Bankston Johnson and Maria, plus Gatschet 1886 and Haas & Swadesh 1934 (Emma Jackson). No dialect distinctions are made beyond Kaufman's remark on a possible dialectal x~f/s variation.

sources.note: p.15 sec.5.1 'Stress': stress in Biloxi 'largely remains a mystery'; Gatschet's and Dorsey's accent marks vary for the same word, but where they agree they often mark the FINAL syllable; word-final stress unusual for Siouan (1st/2nd-syllable norm); possibly due to contact with Choctaw/Chickasaw final pitch accent. p.14: a 'when stressed' = father, unstressed = schwa. p.89 s.v. ksihį: Gatschet distinguishes ksíhi 'crazy' from ksihí 'evening' by stress mark.

sources.citation: Dorsey, James Owen & John R. Swanton. 1912. A Dictionary of the Biloxi and Ofo Languages. BAE Bulletin 47. Washington: GPO. (archive.org dictionaryofbilo0047dors scanned)
sources.note: Intro pp.2-4: phonetic key only; grave accent (vs acute) used by Dorsey 'in almost all cases... over an oral particle and indicates a falling tone'. Item-level remarks only: s.v. xe 'xe affects the accent of the preceding word' (te'di > tedi' xe; kde'xi > kdexi' xe); s.v. yehon 'na attracts the accent'. No general statement of where accent falls.
